name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q01 - Match root types and modifications to plants

questiontext.text:
Match the root types or modifications with their corresponding plant examples and select the correct combination.

Root Type / Modification Plant Example
A. Fibrous root system (i) Sugarcane
B. Prop roots (ii) Rhizophora
C. Stilt roots (iii) Wheat
D. Pneumatophores (iv) Banyan tree

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Roots in angiosperms are classified based on their origin and may undergo morphological modifications for mechanical support, food storage, or respiration.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
1. Fibrous root system: In monocotyledonous plants such as wheat, the primary root is short-lived and replaced by a large number of roots originating from the base of the stem.
2. Prop roots: In a banyan tree, hanging pillar-like roots grow downwards from horizontal branches to provide mechanical support.
3. Stilt roots: In plants such as maize and sugarcane, supporting roots arise obliquely from the lower nodes of the stem.
4. Pneumatophores: In plants growing in swampy areas such as Rhizophora, roots grow vertically upwards out of the ground to obtain oxygen for respiration.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct biological pairings are: Fibrous root system with wheat, Prop roots with banyan tree, Stilt roots with sugarcane, and Pneumatophores with Rhizophora, which corresponds to A-(iii), B-(iv), C-(i), D-(ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q02 - Match phyllotaxy and leaf types to plants

questiontext.text:
Match the leaf arrangement or leaf type with the corresponding plant example and select the correct combination.

Leaf Feature Plant Example
A. Alternate phyllotaxy (i) Silk cotton
B. Opposite phyllotaxy (ii) Alstonia
C. Whorled phyllotaxy (iii) China rose
D. Palmately compound leaf (iv) Calotropis

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Phyllotaxy describes the pattern of arrangement of leaves on a stem or branch, while compound leaves are classified based on whether leaflets are arranged along a rachis or attached at a common point.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
1. Alternate phyllotaxy: A single leaf arises at each node in an alternate manner, as seen in china rose, mustard, and sunflower.
2. Opposite phyllotaxy: A pair of leaves arises at each node and lies opposite to each other, as in Calotropis and guava.
3. Whorled phyllotaxy: More than two leaves arise at a single node forming a whorl, as in Alstonia.
4. Palmately compound leaf: All leaflets are attached at a common point at the tip of the petiole, as seen in silk cotton.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each leaf feature with its example gives A-(iii), B-(iv), C-(ii), D-(i).

questiontext.text:
Match the stem modifications with their respective functions and plant examples, and choose the correct combination.

Stem Modification Plant Example
A. Underground stem for food storage and perennation (i) Bougainvillea
B. Axillary bud modified into spirally coiled tendril (ii) Opuntia
C. Axillary bud modified into woody, pointed thorn (iii) Zaminkand
D. Flattened chlorophyllous stem for photosynthesis (iv) Grapevine

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Stems can be modified to perform specialized functions such as food storage, climbing support, protection from browsing animals, and photosynthesis in arid habitats.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
1. Underground stem for storage and perennation: Underground stems of potato, ginger, turmeric, zaminkand, and Colocasia store food and act as organs of perennation.
2. Stem tendril: Slender, spirally coiled tendrils developing from axillary buds help plants climb, as seen in gourds and grapevine.
3. Thorn: Woody, straight, and pointed thorns derived from axillary buds protect plants such as Citrus and Bougainvillea from browsing animals.
4. Flattened photosynthetic stem: Arid-region plants like Opuntia modify their stems into flattened, chlorophyll-containing structures to carry out photosynthesis.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The accurate pairing of stem modifications to plant examples is A-(iii), B-(iv), C-(i), D-(ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q04 - Match leaf modifications to plant examples

questiontext.text:
Match the leaf modifications with the corresponding plant examples and select the correct combination.

Leaf Modification Plant Example
A. Leaves converted into tendrils for climbing (i) Garlic
B. Leaves modified into spines for defence (ii) Australian acacia
C. Fleshy leaves storing food (iii) Pea
D. Petioles expanding to synthesise food (iv) Cacti

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Leaves may undergo structural modifications to perform functions beyond photosynthesis, such as climbing support, mechanical defence, food storage, or compensating for short-lived leaf blades.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
1. Leaf tendrils: In plants such as pea, leaves are converted into tendrils to assist in climbing.
2. Leaf spines: In xerophytic plants like cacti, leaves are modified into spines for defence and water conservation.
3. Fleshy storage leaves: Onion and garlic possess fleshy leaves that store reserve food.
4. Expanded photosynthetic petioles: In Australian acacia, the leaves are small and short-lived, so the petioles expand, turn green, and synthesise food.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each modification with its plant example yields A-(iii), B-(iv), C-(i), D-(ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q05 - Match floral symmetry and ovary position to plants

questiontext.text:
Match the floral characteristics with the corresponding plant examples and select the correct combination.

Floral Characteristic Plant Example
A. Actinomorphic flower (i) Canna
B. Zygomorphic flower (ii) Cucumber
C. Asymmetric (irregular) flower (iii) Datura
D. Epigynous flower (inferior ovary) (iv) Cassia

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Flowers are classified by symmetry (radial, bilateral, or irregular) and by the relative position of the calyx, corolla, and androecium with respect to the ovary on the thalamus.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
1. Actinomorphic flower: Can be divided into two equal radial halves in any radial plane passing through the centre, as in mustard, Datura, and chilli.
2. Zygomorphic flower: Can be divided into two similar halves only in one particular vertical plane, as in pea, gulmohur, bean, and Cassia.
3. Asymmetric flower: Cannot be divided into two similar halves by any vertical plane passing through the centre, as in canna.
4. Epigynous flower: The margin of the thalamus grows upward enclosing the ovary completely and fusing with it so other floral parts arise above the inferior ovary, as in guava, cucumber, and ray florets of sunflower.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Pairing each floral feature with its correct plant example gives A-(iii), B-(iv), C-(i), D-(ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q06 - Match aestivation types to plant examples

questiontext.text:
Match the types of aestivation in corolla with their corresponding plant examples and select the correct combination.

Type of Aestivation Plant Example
A. Valvate (i) Pea
B. Twisted (ii) Gulmohur
C. Imbricate (iii) Calotropis
D. Vexillary (iv) Cotton

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Aestivation refers to the mode of arrangement of sepals or petals in a floral bud with respect to the other members of the same whorl.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
1. Valvate aestivation: Sepals or petals in a whorl just touch one another at the margin without overlapping, as in Calotropis.
2. Twisted aestivation: One margin of each appendage overlaps that of the next one consistently in one direction, as in china rose, lady's finger, and cotton.
3. Imbricate aestivation: Margins overlap one another, but not in any particular direction, as in Cassia and gulmohur.
4. Vexillary aestivation: The largest posterior petal (standard) overlaps two lateral wings, which in turn overlap two smallest anterior keel petals, as in pea and bean.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct correspondence is A-(iii), B-(iv), C-(ii), D-(i).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q07 - Match placentation descriptions and plant examples

questiontext.text:
Match the placentation descriptions with their corresponding types and plant examples, and select the correct combination.

Ovary & Placenta Feature Placentation Type & Example
A. Placenta forms a ridge along the ventral suture bearing two rows of ovules (i) Free central; Dianthus
B. Placenta is axial in a multilocular ovary (ii) Parietal; Argemone
C. Ovules develop on the inner wall; ovary may become two-chambered via false septum (iii) Marginal; Pea
D. Ovules borne on central axis and septa are absent (iv) Axile; Lemon

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Placentation is the arrangement of ovules within the ovary, determined by the position of the placenta and the presence or absence of septa.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
1. Ventral suture ridge with two rows of ovules: This defines marginal placentation, characteristically seen in pea.
2. Axial placenta in a multilocular ovary: This defines axile placentation, found in china rose, tomato, and lemon.
3. Ovules on the inner wall with a false septum: In parietal placentation, ovules develop on the inner peripheral wall of a one-chambered ovary that becomes two-chambered due to a false septum, as in mustard and Argemone.
4. Ovules on a central axis without septa: This defines free central placentation, observed in Dianthus and Primrose.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each structural description to its placentation type and example yields A-(iii), B-(iv), C-(ii), D-(i).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q08 - Match stamen and seed features to plants

questiontext.text:
Match the reproductive and seed features with the corresponding plant examples and select the correct combination.

Morphological Feature Plant Example
A. Epiphyllous stamens (i) Citrus
B. Monoadelphous stamens (ii) Castor
C. Polyadelphous stamens (iii) Lily
D. Endospermous dicotyledonous seed (iv) China rose

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Stamens show adhesion to other floral whorls (epipetalous or epiphyllous) or cohesion among themselves (monoadelphous, diadelphous, or polyadelphous), while dicotyledonous seeds are classified as endospermic or non-endospermous based on the persistence of endosperm.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
1. Epiphyllous stamens: Stamens attached to the perianth are termed epiphyllous, as seen in flowers of lily.
2. Monoadelphous stamens: Stamens united into one bunch or bundle occur in china rose.
3. Polyadelphous stamens: Stamens united into more than two bundles are found in citrus.
4. Endospermous dicotyledonous seed: Unlike bean, gram, and pea (which are non-endospermous), castor retains endosperm formed by double fertilisation as a food-storing tissue in mature seeds.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct biological pairings are A-(iii), B-(iv), C-(i), D-(ii).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_MORPHOLOGYOFFLOWERINGPLANTS_MCQ_Q09 - Match angiosperm families to floral traits and economic plants

questiontext.text:
Match the angiosperm families with their diagnostic floral characters and economically important plant examples, and select the correct combination.

Plant Family Diagnostic Floral Character & Example
A. Fabaceae (i) Epitepalous stamens, tricarpellary syncarpous ovary; Colchicum autumnale
B. Solanaceae (ii) Tetramerous corolla, \(\text{A}_{2+4}\) stamens; Mustard
C. Liliaceae (iii) Papilionaceous corolla, diadelphous stamens; Indigofera
D. Brassicaceae (iv) Epipetalous stamens, obliquely placed bicarpellary ovary; Ashwagandha

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Angiosperm families are distinguished by characteristic combinations of floral symmetry, perianth/calyx-corolla structure, stamen arrangement, and gynoecium organisation, along with economically important species.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Pairing
1. Fabaceae: Characterised by zygomorphic flowers with papilionaceous corolla (vexillary aestivation) and ten diadelphous stamens \(\text{A}_{(9)+1}\); Indigofera (a dye source) belongs to this family.
2. Solanaceae: Characterised by actinomorphic flowers with five epipetalous stamens and a bicarpellary, syncarpous, obliquely placed superior ovary with swollen axile placentae; ashwagandha (a medicinal plant) belongs here.
3. Liliaceae: A monocotyledonous family featuring six tepals \((3+3)\), six epitepalous stamens, and a tricarpellary syncarpous superior ovary; Colchicum autumnale (source of colchicine) belongs here.
4. Brassicaceae: Represented by mustard, having the floral formula \(\oplus \, \text{⚥} \, \text{K}_{2+2} \, \text{C}_4 \, \text{A}_{2+4} \, \underline{\text{G}}_{(2)}\) with four free petals and tetradynamous \((2+4)\) stamens.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Matching each family with its diagnostic floral characters and plant example gives A-(iii), B-(iv), C-(i), D-(ii).
